title: The Almoravids and Almohads
hookLine: reforming movements from the Sahara and the Atlas that ruled North Africa and Spain

cards: Ibn Khaldun wrote the history of two movements from his own corner of the world. First, out of the Sahara: a preacher among desert tribes, men who veil their faces, a small band devoted to prayer and strict living.
In time they rule from the desert to al-Andalus. Then, out of the Atlas Mountains: another preacher, another band, sure the rulers have gone soft, who sweep down and replace them.
Two waves of renewal, each coming in from the edge, each with the same promise: we'll bring things back to how they should be.

teach.h: AL-MURABITUN — THE PEOPLE OF THE RIBAT.
teach.b: The Almoravids, in Arabic al-Murabitun, began with a teacher named Abd Allah ibn Yasin preaching among the Sanhaja Berbers of the Sahara.
Tradition ties the name to the ribat, a fortified retreat where people lived for prayer and for defense. Their strength was discipline and the Maliki law, followed closely.
They founded Marrakesh, and under Yusuf ibn Tashfin they crossed the sea when Muslim rulers in al-Andalus, under pressure from Christian kingdoms to the north, asked for help.

The Almohads, al-Muwahhidun, took a name meaning those who affirm the oneness of God, tawhid. Their founder, Ibn Tumart, preached in the Atlas that the Almoravids had grown too fond of law books and too lax in faith.
His followers took Marrakesh and became the new rulers of North Africa and al-Andalus. Under them, Ibn Rushd, whom you met earlier, served as a judge and physician.
The honest part: both movements began as calls to renewal, and both were strict. The Almohad years were hard for Jews and Christians in their lands, and some families left.
And both, in their turn, softened, divided and were replaced. Ibn Khaldun saw his pattern in it. The Qur'an speaks of a community that calls others to good.
In Pickthall's translation: "And there may spring from you a nation who invite to goodness, and enjoin right conduct and forbid indecency." A movement can take a verse like that as its calling.
Ibn Khaldun's history asks what comes after: whether the bond that carried a movement to power holds once it is there.

how: The Almoravids and Almohads are remembered in North Africa through cities and buildings such as Marrakesh, and through the Maliki law and the teaching of tawhid that each emphasized.

games.q: you're a Muslim ruler in al-Andalus, under pressure from Christian kingdoms to the north. across the sea is a strict desert movement with a strong army. what do you do?
o: ask the desert movement to cross over and help.
games.why: rulers in al-Andalus asked the Almoravids for help. they came, and in time they ruled al-Andalus themselves.

practice: Bring to mind one thing in your life that has grown soft or careless and needs renewing: a habit, a promise, a prayer you've let slide. Then ask a second question: could you renew it without turning hard on the people around you?
If you pray, ask for renewal with humility; if you don't, choose one small thing to begin again.

wordCard.voice: Tawhid. The affirming of God's oneness that named the Almohads, one of two reforming movements, with the Almoravids, that ruled North Africa and al-Andalus in turn. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: affirming God's oneness; the idea behind the Almohads' name, al-Muwahhidun.
